name: Chloe Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the business reporter for the regional daily, so I cover local firms: factory openings, shop closures, the chamber of commerce breakfasts and the quarterly jobs figures. A typical day is two or three calls with business owners, a visit to a site if I'm lucky, and writing four stories, one of which is usually a company's results turned into plain English. I like meeting people who've built something from nothing. What wears me down is the pay and how many stories are just rewritten press releases.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, who's an electrician, and we're getting married next September at the church I grew up in. We rent a small flat and we're saving for the wedding, which means we've basically got nothing spare. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise long company reports, but I always check it against the original.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that saves a bit of time, and businesses that use it sensibly will do fine. I'd probably write a piece on which local firms actually got value from it. I wouldn't be dramatic about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel mostly okay. My section is sponsored by a local bank, so it's one of the safer bits of the paper. The real pressure is money at home, because the wedding is eating every spare pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summarising tool now and then and carry on as I am. I'd ask the editor whether I could pick up a monthly business supplement for a bit extra. Daniel and I would keep the wedding to sixty guests instead of a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, calm about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Daniel decide who to cut from the guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly work friends and distant cousins, which my mother wouldn't love. Daniel's side is huge, so he'd have the harder job. We'd sit down with a list on a Sunday afternoon and argue nicely about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the bank sponsorship guaranteed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's renewed every year, so no. If they pulled it, the business pages would shrink to one a day. That's the thing that would really worry me.

say: AI is a **useful tool** that saves time, and sensible businesses will do fine.
She'd write about which **local firms** actually got value from it.
think: Her section is **sponsored** by a local bank, making it one of the safer parts of the paper.
The real pressure is the **wedding** eating every spare pound.
do: Keep using the **summarising tool** now and then and carry on as normal.
Ask to write a **monthly business supplement** for extra pay.
Cut the wedding to **sixty guests** instead of a hundred.
feel: **Uneasy** about money but calm about the job.
S0.quote: My section is sponsored by a local bank, so it's one of the safer bits of the paper.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **fairly safe**, so unease rather than anxiety fits.
Money strain comes from the **wedding**, not from her work.
Her sponsorship safety depends on a **yearly renewal**, which she knows.

steps.text: Keep covering local firms and use AI summaries now and then
Pitch a paid monthly business supplement to the editor
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses will use AI to stay competitive, and that's their right, but readers still want a human who'll ask the hard question at the results briefing. I'd write about local firms adapting. I'd stay positive in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my job is turning company results and press releases into stories, and a machine can do that easily. I think the paper would cut the business desk to me plus a machine, or merge it with the city paper's. My job wouldn't vanish overnight, but my hours or my role could shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen other business desks do it well, I'd learn the tools properly so I can do twice the stories with better checks. I'd also look at communications jobs at local manufacturers, which pay better. Daniel and I would still get married, but we'd put the house deposit plan back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit cross with myself for not having a plan already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses have the right to use AI. Would you say that if it was your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would, yes. I don't believe in stopping firms from doing what keeps them going. I'd just want the paper to be straight with us about it, and to give people a fair chance to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your vicar or church friends about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm worried but trusting. Our church runs a jobs club on Tuesday mornings, mostly for older people who lost factory jobs. I might end up helping with it, or needing it.

say: Businesses have the **right** to use AI to stay competitive.
Readers still want a human to ask the **hard question** at a results briefing.
think: Turning **results and press releases** into stories is easy for a machine.
The business desk could shrink to **one person** plus a machine, or merge.
do: Learn the tools properly **once other desks** show it works.
Look at **communications jobs** at local manufacturers.
Delay the **house deposit** plan by a year.
feel: **Anxious**, and cross with herself for having no plan already.
S1.quote: A lot of my job is turning company results and press releases into stories, and a machine can do that easily.
fieldNote: Her **free-market** belief holds even when it threatens her job.
Church **jobs club** shows community as her safety net.
AI is shifting **household plans**: the house deposit gets pushed back.

steps.text: Learn AI tools for business news once other desks prove them
Apply for communications jobs at local manufacturers
Push the house deposit plan back by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches will need to look after each other, because this is too fast for government. I'd say businesses need to think about their people, not just costs. That's what I'd say at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028, because everything I do is thinking work. Daniel's job is hands-on, wiring and fitting, so he'd have until about 2031. Electricians might even be busy for a while, wiring up all the new data centres and robot lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding right down to the registry office and a church blessing, and keep the money as savings. I'd look for any job that uses people skills and isn't just screen work, like helping Daniel run his jobs and talking to his customers. I'd probably start an apprenticeship in electrical work myself, since there'd be three years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I keep thinking about how much we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about cutting the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly, I've pictured it since I was little. But the marriage matters more than the party. My nan got married in her best dress with sandwiches in the church hall, and she was married sixty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really start an electrical apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if Daniel took me on. I'm not squeamish and I'm good with detail. It's a practical skill and practical skills would last longer.

say: **Families and churches** will need to look after each other, as this is too fast for government.
Businesses should think about **their people**, not just costs.
think: Her job is **gone by 2028**, because it's all thinking work.
Her fiancé's **hands-on** wiring work lasts until about 2031, and might even boom.
do: Shrink the wedding to a **registry office** and church blessing and save the rest.
Help her fiancé **run his jobs** and talk to customers.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** in the three years before robots.
feel: **Scared**, thinking of how much they'd planned.
S2.quote: The marriage matters more than the party.
fieldNote: She spots that **electricians** may stay busy wiring data centres and robot lines.
The **3-year robot gap** drives her idea of a hands-on apprenticeship.
Wedding cuts are **painful** but rooted in her nan's example.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to a registry office and church blessing
Run customer calls and bookings for her fiancé's electrical work
Start an electrical apprenticeship with her fiancé
Save the cancelled wedding budget as an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives firms and families time to prepare, so nobody should be caught out. I'd write about local businesses that train their own people. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means we'd get married as planned and I'd still have a job for a while. My writing job goes by 2031. But I'd have time to build something with Daniel instead of scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep the job, get married, and use AI more at work so I'm faster. Then I'd do a bookkeeping course in the evenings so I could run the office side of Daniel's business. We'd save hard for a van and tools for a second electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a hopeful kind of way. We'd be building together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bookkeeping is thinking work too. Wouldn't AI take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a lot of it, yes. But running a small firm is more than the books: chasing customers, ordering, keeping the lads happy. I'd use AI for the sums and do the people side myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wedding goes ahead. What changes about married life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a few years on children until the business is steady. That's hard to say, because my mother is already asking. But I'd rather be ready than rushed.

say: Five years gives firms and families **time to prepare**.
**Apprenticeships** matter more than ever, she'd say in print.
think: They'd **marry as planned** and she'd keep her job for a while.
Her writing job **goes by 2031**, but there's time to build with her fiancé.
do: Use **AI more** at work to get faster in the first year.
Take an evening **bookkeeping course** to run the office side.
Save for a **van and tools** for a second electrician.
feel: **Anxious** but hopeful, because they'd be building together.
S3.quote: Running a small firm is more than the books: chasing customers, ordering, keeping the lads happy.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **plan a family business** instead of scrambling.
Admits **bookkeeping** is exposed too, and splits work between AI and people.
Delaying **children** is a quiet but real cost.

steps.text: Use AI tools more on the business desk to work faster
Save for a van and tools for a second electrician
Wait a few years before having children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good long time for businesses, schools and churches to help people move on. I'd write a hopeful piece about it. I'd say hard work and planning will get most people through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly settled about this one. Ten years means I could keep reporting, have children, and slowly move across to running the business with Daniel. My reporting job would still end, but on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for several years and learn the AI tools well. I'd do the bookkeeping course and help Daniel on Saturdays so the move is gradual. We'd marry next year as planned, and maybe start a family in three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at times, but mostly peaceful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said mostly peaceful. Does money still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, money always does, we've got almost nothing saved and a wedding coming. But with ten years I think we'd build a cushion. I'd aim for three months by the time any children come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young people at church thinking about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young people at church to learn a trade or a skill you can do with your hands, as well as any degree. I'd want them to hear it from someone who didn't.

say: Ten years is long enough for **businesses, schools and churches** to help people move on.
**Hard work** and planning will get most people through.
think: She'd feel **fairly settled**, with time for children and a gradual move.
Her reporting job would still end, but **on her terms**.
do: Keep her job **several years** and learn the AI tools well.
Help her fiancé on **Saturdays** to make the move gradual.
Build **three months** of savings before children come.
S4.quote: My reporting job would still end, but on my terms.
fieldNote: The decade lets her see a **settled future**, so mood eases to uneasy.
Household cover from her fiancé's **trade** keeps worry lower than her job alone would.
Her advice to **young people** reflects her own regret.

steps.text: Keep the business reporting job for several more years
Learn AI tools well for business reporting
Save three months of expenses before having children
Marry next September and plan children in three or four years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as we're getting married and before we've saved anything. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults and support for small trades businesses so Daniel could take me or others on. And churches and community groups getting help to run proper jobs clubs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how this feels for people of faith. I think a lot of us would lean on our churches and mosques more than on the government. That's not a bad thing, but those places would need help too.

headlineQuote: A lot of us would lean on our churches and mosques more than on the government.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old business reporter** at a regional daily, engaged to an electrician and saving for a church wedding.
She uses AI **now and then**, believes firms should be free to use it, and moves once others prove it.
She's **uneasy** in AI Plateau, anxious as desk work shrinks, and **alarmed** under AGI by 2028.
Her fallback is building a **family business** with her fiancé, using his trade and the robot gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would hit just as she marries and before they've saved.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships** and support for small trades businesses.
Help for churches and **community groups** to run proper jobs clubs.
